clue.text: Arch Jot Findlayson, Hitchcock and Co in the Day's work

definitions.text: Arch Jot Findlayson, Hitchcock and Co in the Day's work

blocks.clueFragment: Arch Jot Findlayson, Hitchcock and Co
blocks.note: surface reading: an odd list of names, as if a firm's letterhead
setter's reading: Findlayson and Hitchcock are the engineers in a Kipling story from his collection The Day's Work, building an arched span over the Ganges

explanation.surface: A roll-call of colleagues going about an ordinary day at work.
explanation.walkthrough: The Day's Work is a Kipling collection; its story The Bridge-Builders follows the engineer Findlayson and his assistant Hitchcock. 'Arch' hints at what they build.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the Kipling story names exactly the profession of its two engineering heroes, who erect a great railway crossing.

blocks.note: to bar is to prohibit
an ouch is an old word for a brooch or clasp

explanation.surface: A ban on buckles fitted to coaches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clasps' reads as a verb, but it is a plural noun: OUCH is an archaic word for a jewelled clasp.
explanation.definitionFit: A barouche is a four-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle with a folding hood, so the plural names such vehicles.

definitions.note: describes timber identified by its grain, read as IN GRAIN

blocks.note: first meaning: wood is known ..., by its pattern of fibres
second meaning: dyed in the fibre, so thoroughly fixed

explanation.surface: Timber you can identify, as if it were thoroughly dyed.
explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words the answer describes wood known by its grain; as one word it means dyed through.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingrain describes colour fixed in the fibre before weaving, hence thoroughly or permanently coloured, deeply rooted.

definitions.note: 22 is DUKEDOM, so this means a dukedom

blocks.note: first meaning: a hard English cheese, single or double
second meaning: the answer to 22 down is a title held by a duke, and this county gives its name to one

explanation.surface: A cheese produced in some unnamed place numbered 22.
explanation.walkthrough: Gloucester is an English county known for its cheese, and the Duke of Gloucester is a royal title.
explanation.definitionFit: Double Gloucester is a well-known English hard cheese, and the royal title Duke of Gloucester makes the county a ducal territory.

clue.text: With divided opinions even so young!

definitions.text: With divided opinions even so young!

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who is undecided, who sits on the fence
setter's reading: a fledgling bird perched undecided on its ledge, not yet ready to fly

explanation.surface: Someone so young already finds their views split.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is on a chick that has not yet committed to leaving the nest, like a person who cannot make up their mind.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird not yet feathered for flight is immature, so the word also describes an inexperienced youngster.

definitions.note: a woman's name stands for an individual

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra
taken as written

explanation.surface: A declaration that a pound coin counts as a human being.
explanation.definitionFit: Lisa is a woman's first name, standing for an individual human being in the loose way crossword names do.

clue.text: Some preferred the land of roast beef to the French chop

definitions.text: Some preferred the land of roast beef to the French chop

blocks.clueFragment: Some preferred the land of roast beef to the French chop
blocks.note: surface reading: diners who chose English beef over a French cut of meat
setter's reading: the chop is the guillotine, and the land of roast beef is England, where French nobles fled

explanation.surface: A menu choice between English roast beef and a French cutlet.
explanation.walkthrough: England is 'the land of roast beef', after the old patriotic song; the French aristocrats who escaped the Revolution's guillotine settled there.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names people who leave their own country, classically the nobles who left France during the Revolution.

definitions.note: a phrase describing a place rather than a noun, fair because the town really is of Bedfordshire, so the name answers 'one of Beds'

blocks.note: first meaning: having light reddish-yellow hair
second meaning: a familiar name for a Scotsman, short for Alexander
third meaning: a market town in Bedfordshire, an English county abbreviated Beds

explanation.surface: A fair-haired Scotsman described as belonging to some beds.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings: a hair colour, a nickname for a Scot, and a town in Bedfordshire, an English county whose abbreviation looks like furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes ginger-blond colouring, serves as a stock nickname for Scotsmen, and names a Bedfordshire market town.

clue.text: Forty winks up — Eve got on with the work

definitions.text: Eve got on with the work
definitions.note: the definition is the verb, past tense of spin, as in 'When Adam delved and Eve span'

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from the bottom of the column to the top

blocks.note: forty winks are short sleeps

explanation.surface: Eve skips her afternoon nap to get on with her chores.
explanation.walkthrough: The old rhyme 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?' gives the archaic past tense of spin.
explanation.definitionFit: Span is the old past tense of spin, and spinning thread was the household labour the rhyme assigns to Eve.

clue.text: Pull yourselves together again, one chap has a fowl infection

blocks.note: Reg is a man's name, short for Reginald
roup is a respiratory disease of poultry

explanation.surface: A call to rally the team, though one member's chicken has caught something.
explanation.definitionFit: To regroup is to reassemble or reorganise after a setback, recovering composure as a unit.

blocks.note: first meaning: a thick twilled cotton cloth
second meaning: pompous, inflated language

explanation.surface: It will serve as padding, since 'Twill' reads as the contraction of 'it will'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twill' looks like the old contraction for 'it will'; it is the woven fabric. Bombast originally meant cotton padding, so both senses come from cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a coarse twilled fabric and, figuratively, high-flown speech that is all stuffing and no substance.

blocks.note: surface reading: a situation that is not especially sharp or serious
setter's reading: the marks over vowels in French, so a syllable carrying no such mark and no stress

explanation.surface: Describing something not particularly critical or serious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acute' and 'grave' look like words about severity, but they are the names of written accent marks.
explanation.definitionFit: A syllable without stress, or a letter without a diacritic mark, lacks emphasis in speech or writing.

blocks.note: first meaning: a fight or brawl
second meaning: to come apart into threads at the edge

explanation.surface: A fragment of a piece by the composer Ravel.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital R makes Ravel look like the French composer, and 'Scrap' like a snippet of music.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a noisy fight, and as a verb it means to unravel or wear thin at the edges.

blocks.note: surface reading: some comparison with a man named Creasy and his fights
setter's reading: Sir Edward Creasy wrote The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World, so the opposite of his subjects

explanation.surface: Something unlike the struggles of a person called Creasy.
explanation.walkthrough: Creasy's 1851 history The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World was a standard Victorian book; whatever is unlike those battles settles nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes an outcome that fails to settle a matter, the reverse of the conclusive engagements Creasy chose.

clue.text: Writer at Belshazzar's feast observed to be no hawk

blocks.note: at Belshazzar's feast a disembodied hand wrote on the wall
saw means observed

explanation.surface: Someone at a biblical banquet was watched and judged not to be a bird of prey.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says 'I know a hawk from a handsaw', so this tool is the thing that is no hawk.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet contrasts the bird of prey with this carpenter's tool, so the tool is literally what a hawk is not.

blocks.note: surface reading: a dealer in scrap metal
setter's reading: a scrap is a fight, so this merchant deals in conflict

explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like waste metal, but it means a fight; a monger is a dealer, as in fishmonger.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who stirs up and promotes armed conflict is, figuratively, a trader peddling fights.

clue.text: A heritable unit's is in the beginning

blocks.note: a gene is a unit of heredity, and the possessive adds S
taken as written

explanation.surface: A biology statement about what a gene's role is at the start of life.
explanation.walkthrough: The (4,3) enumeration matches the wordplay split rather than the single word. The first book of the Bible opens with 'In the beginning'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means origin or creation, and is the name of the first book of the Bible, which tells of creation.

blocks.note: surface reading: hills shaped like the letter S
setter's reading: the letter S and some hills, so S 'and' hills, with hills as dunes

explanation.surface: Serpentine hills on the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'S hills' as 'S and hills': the letter S, then AND, then a word for coastal hills.
explanation.definitionFit: Dunes are mounds of windblown grains heaped along a beach, the typical coastal hill.

clue.text: Never the stuff of Julia's reticule

definitions.text: Never the stuff of Julia's reticule

blocks.clueFragment: Never the stuff of Julia's reticule
blocks.note: surface reading: something a lady named Julia would never keep in her handbag
setter's reading: the material a reticule, a lady's silk purse, is made from, which proverbially can never be this

explanation.surface: An item you would never find in a genteel woman's handbag.
explanation.walkthrough: A reticule is a small drawstring purse; the proverb says 'You can't make a silk purse out of a sow's ear'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb names this pig's body part as the material that can never be turned into a fine silk bag.

blocks.note: first meaning: standing in line until one's turn
second meaning: attending on diners at table, as a waiter does

explanation.surface: Standing in line to be served.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one idea, people in line to be served, but the word also means doing the serving.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means staying put until one's turn comes, and also the job of serving food at table.

blocks.note: first meaning: the fine porcelain china made near this place, notoriously fragile
second meaning: the capital of Saxony in Germany

explanation.surface: A city regretted for how easily it can be broken.
explanation.walkthrough: Dresden china is the delicate porcelain of Meissen, near the German city of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The German city's name is used for its delicate porcelain figurines, and it is itself the capital of Saxony.

clue.text: Prospero's library was this enough, he said

definitions.text: Prospero's library was this enough, he said

blocks.clueFragment: Prospero's library was this enough, he said
blocks.note: surface reading: a man describing his book collection as adequate
setter's reading: in The Tempest Prospero says 'my library was' a certain realm 'large enough'

explanation.surface: A character remarking that his books were sufficient for him.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation from The Tempest, Act 1, has the word 'large' between the answer and 'enough'; Prospero was Duke of Milan.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero, deposed ruler of Milan, valued his books as much as the ducal territory he lost.

blocks.note: first meaning: terrifying
second meaning: literally growing locks again on a bare scalp

explanation.surface: A complaint that a baldness cure is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for terrifying is taken literally: a remedy for baldness lifts new growth on the scalp.
explanation.definitionFit: Something terrifying makes the hair stand on end, so the idiom means extremely scary or alarming.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone paying for a piece of mail
setter's reading: one who lets out property, a landlord, who is paid by the tenant

explanation.surface: A man paying for a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' looks like correspondence, but it means one who lets; the person renting pays the one letting.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rents goods or property pays the owner who lets them out.

clue.text: Thomas gave the glad eye beguilingly (to Miss Kilmansegg ?)

definitions.note: an adverb for a past-tense verb, deceived

blocks.note: Thomas Hood, the Victorian comic poet
to give someone the glad eye is to wink at them flirtatiously

explanation.surface: A man flirting charmingly with a lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hood wrote the comic poem Miss Kilmansegg and Her Precious Leg, which explains the bracketed hint.
explanation.definitionFit: To be deceived or tricked is to be led astray by charm, the sense of beguiling.

blocks.note: surface reading: a fresh-faced young man
setter's reading: a surname, the young hero of Hardy's Under the Greenwood Tree

explanation.walkthrough: In Thomas Hardy's Under the Greenwood Tree the young hero's surname is Dewy, so the clue asks for his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The young lover in Hardy's novel is called by this first name, also old slang for any fellow.

blocks.note: first meaning: old British small coins, like the threepenny piece, before decimal money
second meaning: the metal mouthpieces of a bridle

explanation.walkthrough: A threepenny bit was a small pre-decimal British coin worth three pennies.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names old small coins like the threepenny piece and the mouthpieces fitted in a horse's mouth.

blocks.note: C is a musical note
concealed means hidden

explanation.surface: Someone told off for hiding a message.
explanation.definitionFit: Chidden is the old past participle of chide, to rebuke or reprimand someone.

clue.text: Office of royal touchdown at Rugby

blocks.note: Latin for 'of the king', as in Bognor Regis
a try is scored by grounding the ball over the line in rugby

explanation.surface: A department handling royal scoring at Rugby School.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby with a capital R is the school where the game was born; a try is rugby's touchdown.
explanation.definitionFit: A registry is a place where official records are kept, such as a register office for weddings.

blocks.note: surface reading: a diplomat who has been arrested or broken many times
setter's reading: often portrayed in carved busts, as on the square pillars called herms

explanation.walkthrough: Herms, pillars topped with a carved head, were named after this god, the messenger of Olympus.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god served as messenger of the gods, and his carved head topped countless roadside pillars.
